mentions.quote: Thirteen sons have been stated by Manu of old.
mentions.role: cited authority on the classification of sons

mentions.quote: Gambling was forbidden by Manu as it destroys truth, purity, and wealth
mentions.role: cited authority prohibiting gambling

mentions.quote: Because it is connected to the meaning of the Veda, the pre-eminence of Manu is remembered. A Smṛti that is contrary to the meaning of Manu is not to be praised.
mentions.role: supreme legislative authority whose rulings define valid Smṛti

entities.description: The primordial lawgiver whose rulings on sons, gambling, and dharma are cited as authoritative throughout this section.
entities.justification: Manu is explicitly named in three paragraphs as the source of specific legal rulings on inheritance and gambling, and his pre-eminence among Smṛti authors is affirmed at the close of Book 1.

mentions.quote: Having worshipped Agni and Prajāpati, she is made so, said Gautama.
mentions.role: cited legal authority on the ritual making of an appointed daughter

entities.description: An ancient sage and dharmaśāstra authority cited for the ritual procedure by which a daughter is appointed as a son-substitute.
entities.justification: Gautama is named as the source of the ruling that a daughter is 'made' an appointed daughter through worship of Agni and Prajāpati.

mentions.quote: A tenth for one with many protectors, a fifth for one with few; all of it for one without son, father, or wife—thus says Śaunaka.
mentions.role: cited authority on the king's share of a deceased's estate

entities.description: An ancient sage cited as the source of graduated rules for the king's entitlement to inheritance from heirless persons.
entities.justification: Śaunaka is explicitly attributed as the source of the rule regarding proportional shares of heirless estates.

mentions.quote: Having worshipped Agni and Prajāpati, she is made so, said Gautama.
mentions.role: deity invoked in the ritual of appointing a daughter

entities.description: The Vedic fire deity whose worship is part of the ritual by which a daughter is formally appointed as a son-substitute.
entities.justification: Agni is named alongside Prajāpati as a deity to be propitiated in the ritual appointment of a daughter, grounding the act in sacred observance.

mentions.quote: Having worshipped Agni and Prajāpati, she is made so, said Gautama.
mentions.role: deity invoked in the ritual of appointing a daughter

entities.description: The Vedic lord of creatures whose worship, together with Agni, sanctifies the appointment of a daughter as heir.
entities.justification: Prajāpati is explicitly named alongside Agni as a recipient of worship in the rite of appointing a daughter.

mentions.quote: It is ordained for those learned Brahmins who offer the funeral cake to him.
mentions.role: priestly class whose ritual function determines inheritance worthiness

mentions.quote: Sons of a Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, and Shudra wife, born of a Brahmin, in order, should take four, three, two, and one share respectively.
mentions.role: highest-caste father from whom differential inheritance shares are reckoned

mentions.quote: The son of a Brahmin wife should take the land that has come as a gift to a Brahmin.
mentions.role: recipient of gifted land that may not pass to lower-caste sons

mentions.quote: For a Brahmin, branding on the forehead is ordained; no other punishment.
mentions.role: caste category exempt from corporal punishment beyond branding

mentions.quote: the king should examine daily the disputes brought by litigants, and likewise other matters dependent on the king, along with learned Brahmins.
mentions.role: royal advisors in judicial proceedings

entities.description: The priestly varna whose members receive preferential inheritance shares, are exempt from most corporal punishment, and serve as royal judicial advisors.
entities.justification: Brahmins appear throughout the inheritance and punishment sections as the highest-ranked caste with specific legal privileges and ritual functions.

mentions.quote: Sons of a Kshatriya wife take three, two, and one share
mentions.role: second-ranked caste whose sons receive graduated inheritance shares

mentions.quote: For those Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras who are sonless and devoid of wife and brother, the king is the taker of their wealth
mentions.role: caste whose heirless estates pass to the king

entities.description: The warrior and ruling varna whose sons receive three, two, and one shares in the inheritance hierarchy and whose heirless property escheats to the king.
entities.justification: Kshatriyas are consistently ranked second in the inheritance share hierarchy and are included among castes subject to royal escheat of heirless property.

mentions.quote: sons of a Vaishya wife take two and one share
mentions.role: third-ranked caste in inheritance share allocation

mentions.quote: For those Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras who are sonless and devoid of wife and brother, the king is the taker of their wealth
mentions.role: caste whose heirless estates pass to the king

entities.description: The merchant and farming varna whose sons receive two and one share and whose heirless property passes to the king.
entities.justification: Vaishyas are explicitly named in both the inheritance share formula and the royal escheat provision, consistently occupying the third rank.

mentions.quote: A son born of a Shudra woman by one of the twice-born does not deserve a share of the land.
mentions.role: lowest-ranked caste whose sons are excluded from land inheritance

mentions.quote: the son by a Shudra woman, if pure by caste, they are middling; all are remembered as sons entitled to inheritance.
mentions.role: caste whose sons hold an intermediate inheritance status

mentions.quote: to the brother who is the son of a Shudra concubine, they should give a mere token of respect after the father's death
mentions.role: concubine caste whose sons receive only minimal recognition

entities.description: The lowest varna whose sons by twice-born fathers are excluded from land shares and receive only maintenance or token gifts.
entities.justification: Shudras are mentioned repeatedly in the inheritance sections to define the lower boundary of inheritance entitlement based on caste hierarchy.

mentions.quote: A Niṣāda who is the only son of a Brahmin is a sharer of a third part; two parts the kinsmen or sapindas, or the offerer of the funeral oblation, shall take.
mentions.role: mixed-caste son who receives a reduced inheritance fraction

entities.description: A person of mixed Brahmin-and-tribal descent who, as the sole son of a Brahmin, is entitled to only one-third of the inheritance.
entities.justification: The Niṣāda is singled out by name as an exceptional case where mixed descent limits the inheritance fraction to one-third even when the son is the only heir.

mentions.quote: The ancestors, fearing a fall into hell, long for sons, thinking: "Someone who will go to Gayā, he will save us."
mentions.role: sacred pilgrimage site where ancestral rites release ancestors from hell

entities.description: A sacred pilgrimage site in northern India where sons perform ancestral rites (piṇḍa offerings) believed to liberate deceased ancestors from hell.
entities.justification: Gayā is named as the destination a son must visit to save his ancestors from hell, grounding the theological importance of having a male heir.

mentions.quote: And rites such as the Vaiśvadeva must be done by the undivided.
mentions.role: household ritual obligation binding undivided co-heirs

entities.description: A daily Vedic household fire ritual offered to all the gods (Viśve Devāḥ) that must be performed by undivided family members as a collective obligation.
entities.justification: The Vaiśvadeva is cited as an example of shared ritual obligations that only undivided co-heirs must perform together, distinguishing it from partitioned estates.

mentions.quote: *Strīdhana* belongs to her offspring, and a daughter is a sharer in it, if she is unmarried; but if married, she receives a mere token of respect.
mentions.role: category of women's property governed by special succession rules

entities.description: The category of property belonging exclusively to a woman, heritable by her offspring, with an unmarried daughter as a sharer and a married daughter receiving only a token.
entities.justification: Strīdhana is defined at the opening of this window and its inheritance rules are elaborated as distinct from general estate division.

mentions.quote: Because a son saves his father from the hell called Put, one should strive for his birth, even for the mere sight of his face.
mentions.role: afterlife punishment from which a son redeems his father

entities.description: A hell realm in dharmaśāstra cosmology from which a son (putra) saves his father, providing the etymological and theological basis for the imperative to have male heirs.
entities.justification: Put is named as the specific hell that a son prevents by fulfilling filial duties, making it the soteriological basis for inheritance law's emphasis on sons.

themes.topic: Inheritance rights of women (wife, daughter, widow)

mentions.quote: *Strīdhana* belongs to her offspring, and a daughter is a sharer in it
Like a son, the daughter of men is born from limb to limb; therefore, how can another man take the father's wealth?
the wife is remembered as half the body, equal in the fruit of merit and demerit
The wife is the taker of the husband's wealth; without her, the daughter is remembered as the heir.

themes.justification: Multiple contiguous sections (1.26.8–9, 1.26.12) are devoted to the inheritance entitlements of widows and daughters, establishing a priority order that places the wife first and the daughter second.

themes.topic: Caste hierarchy as determinant of inheritance shares

mentions.quote: Sons of a Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, and Shudra wife, born of a Brahmin, in order, should take four, three, two, and one share respectively.
A son born of a Shudra woman by one of the twice-born does not deserve a share of the land.
A Niṣāda who is the only son of a Brahmin is a sharer of a third part

themes.justification: Throughout the partition sections the text systematically assigns different share fractions based on the caste of the mother, making varna the primary variable in inheritance allocation.

mentions.quote: Because a son saves his father from the hell called Put, one should strive for his birth, even for the mere sight of his face.
The ancestors, fearing a fall into hell, long for sons, thinking: "Someone who will go to Gayā, he will save us."
The grandson and the son of an appointed daughter both cause the attainment of heaven.

themes.justification: The text repeatedly frames the need for male heirs in eschatological terms—sons rescue fathers from hell Put, grandsons secure heaven—making soteriology the theological foundation of succession law.

themes.topic: Partition and re-union of joint family property

mentions.quote: Those two who have reunited out of affection are sharers of each other's property.
He who, having been partitioned, again lives in one place with his father, brother, or paternal uncle out of affection, he is called a reunited co-heir.
A document of proclamation should be made by partitioned brothers among themselves, or irreproachable witnesses should be appointed by those dividing, to prevent disputes.

themes.justification: Section 1.26.10 is devoted entirely to the rules governing reunion of already-partitioned brothers, establishing that re-union creates new joint-property rights that supersede prior partition.

themes.topic: Regulation of gambling and state oversight

mentions.quote: Gambling was forbidden by Manu as it destroys truth, purity, and wealth; but it was permitted by others, accompanied by a share for the king.
The gambling-hall manager is the collector there; he should give to the victor and to the king. The king's share is from the gambler; from the gambling-hall manager, it is ten percent.
Wicked men who play with false dice, and those who withhold the king's share, and those who cheat in counting—those gamblers are remembered as punishable.

themes.justification: Section 1.27 frames gambling as a legally tolerated but king-supervised activity, balancing Manu's prohibition against pragmatic revenue extraction and crime detection.

themes.topic: Graduated royal punishment according to caste and offence

mentions.quote: Verbal censure, reprimand, fine, and capital punishment—the fourfold punishment has been devised. Having known the person, the fault, and his means, one should apply it.
For a Brahmin, branding on the forehead is ordained; no other punishment.
One deserving death deserves a fine of one hundred suvarṇas; for cutting off a limb, half of that; for banishment, twenty-five.

themes.justification: Section 1.29 systematically scales punishment by offence severity and caste identity (Brahmins receive branding rather than corporal punishment), reflecting the text's broader project of calibrated royal justice.

themes.topic: Wife as co-owner and ritual partner of the husband

mentions.quote: the wife is remembered as half the body, equal in the fruit of merit and demerit
When the husband who maintained the sacred fire has died before her, his wealth a devoted wife shall obtain; this is the eternal dharma.
He whose wife has not died, half his body lives; while half the body is living, how can another obtain the wealth?

themes.justification: The text grounds the wife's inheritance right in an ontological claim—she is 'half the body'—making the wife not merely an heir by convention but a co-owner by nature.

themes.topic: Authority of the Veda and Manu as supreme normative sources

mentions.quote: In the Veda, in the treatises of Smṛti, and in worldly custom, by the wise, the wife is remembered as half the body
Because it is connected to the meaning of the Veda, the pre-eminence of Manu is remembered. A Smṛti that is contrary to the meaning of Manu is not to be praised.

themes.justification: The final verse of Book 1 explicitly subordinates all Smṛti literature to the Veda via Manu, making this a meta-legal statement about the hierarchy of legal sources.

themes.topic: Limits on widows' property rights (restricted ownership)

mentions.quote: Even if of good conduct, and even when a share is made, a woman does not deserve immovable property.
for as long as she lives, she has limited ownership in respect of gift, mortgage, and sale.
Whatever of the divided property is remembered from the rule of pledge and so on, that a widow shall obtain, excepting immovable property.

themes.justification: A distinct sub-theme runs through section 1.26.9 qualifying the widow's inheritance with a structural limitation: she receives movable property with full ownership but immovable property only with restricted alienation rights.

themes.topic: Śrāddha (ancestral rites) as legal obligation binding heirs

mentions.quote: having honored them with perfumes and garlands, one should offer them to the one who eats at the śrāddha.
she should cause the monthly, six-monthly, and other śrāddhas to be offered.
for the monthly, six-monthly, or annual śrāddha, with effort.

themes.justification: The text treats performance of śrāddha not merely as a pious duty but as a legal condition that shapes who qualifies as heir; the requirement to fund and conduct ancestral rites implicitly determines inheritance eligibility.

citations.quote: Thirteen sons have been stated by Manu of old.
citations.justification: The text attributes a specific doctrinal position—the enumeration of thirteen types of sons—directly to Manu, treating the Manusmṛti as the authoritative prior source.

citations.quote: Gambling was forbidden by Manu as it destroys truth, purity, and wealth
citations.justification: Manu is cited as the authority behind the prohibition of gambling; the text then records a competing permissive view, framing the passage as an inter-textual jurisprudential debate.

citations.quote: Because it is connected to the meaning of the Veda, the pre-eminence of Manu is remembered. A Smṛti that is contrary to the meaning of Manu is not to be praised.
citations.justification: This closing verse explicitly cites Manu's work as the normative standard against which all other Smṛti texts are to be measured, asserting Manu's canonical pre-eminence.

citations.quote: Having worshipped Agni and Prajāpati, she is made so, said Gautama.
citations.justification: Gautama is cited by name as the source for the ritual procedure of appointing a daughter, indicating Bṛhaspati is drawing on the Gautama Dharmasūtra as a legal precedent.

citations.quote: A tenth for one with many protectors, a fifth for one with few; all of it for one without son, father, or wife—thus says Śaunaka.
citations.justification: Śaunaka is explicitly named as the source of a graduated rule for royal escheat, indicating Bṛhaspati is citing an earlier authoritative text attributed to Śaunaka.
